title: [Security] NotAction/NotResource statements silently model as empty (CWE-693)
body:
Part of tracker #62 (audit key BUG-R2-S1-A5-H6, CVSS 10.0, reproduced on main).

## Summary

_build_statement_condition reads only Action/Resource keys. A statement using NotAction/NotResource (no Action key) yields an empty pattern list, models as logical False with no exception, and vanishes from the proof: a near-admin Allow (NotAction single-read on *) verifies as compliant, verify_access is blind to everything such policies grant, and invisible NotAction-Denies are dropped (false ALLOWED proofs that reach VC ADMIT). TerraformParser passes the keys through untouched (zero occurrences of NotAction anywhere in code/tests/docs). Reproduced live 2026-09-14 (NotAction near-admin → verified=True, allowed=False).

## Anchors

- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:183-209 (empty-list → False coercion, no exception path)
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:211-228 (invisible Allow contributes nothing; invisible Deny dropped)
- qwed_infra/parsers/terraform_parser.py:217-250 (keys never inspected)
- Residue of the #9 fix family (commented on #9)

## Fix direction

Fail closed on unmodeled statement elements: raise on NotAction/NotResource/NotPrincipal in both the guard and the parser (mirroring the unresolved-interpolation refusal), so verify_access returns UNVERIFIABLE instead of guessing. Report includes patch text; treat as starting point, review adversarially.
label: SECURITY

title: [Security] Least-privilege needs existential condition quantification (CWE-693)
body:
Part of tracker #62 (audit key BUG-R2-S1-A2-H5-existential, CVSS 7.1, EXP-confirmed by auditors).

## Summary

Deeper variant of #65: even the probe-context concept is wrong. Conditions must be evaluated existentially ("does ANY request context receive full admin"), but verify_access creates Z3 variables only for action/resource and pins both to constants — the solver has zero freedom to vary condition inputs, so the verdict is fully determined by one synthetic context. Unimplemented operators (Bool, DateGreaterThan, ArnLike, ...) are invisible under EVERY context, so no caller-side multi-probe hardening can see those grants. Complementary to #65 (sampling) and #63/#64 (polarity), not redundant with either.

## Anchors

- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:256-258 (only s_action/s_resource are symbolic; pinned by query)
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:149-165 (unknown operators → False under all contexts)

## Fix direction

Introduce a symbolic request-context variable (String sort is already imported) for existential evaluation, or fail closed to UNVERIFIABLE wherever conditions cannot be proven unsatisfiable. Report sketches condition-stripped probing with conditional-Deny dropping; treat as starting point, review adversarially.
label: SECURITY

title: [Security] Least-privilege probe samples one fixed context; condition-scoped admin passes (CWE-693)
body:
Part of tracker #62 (audit key BUG-R2-S1-A2-H4, CVSS 7.1, reproduced on main).

## Summary

verify_least_privilege answers "does this policy allow full admin" by sampling ONE hard-wired request context (SourceIp 0.0.0.0, CurrentTime 2100-01-01). Any "Allow * on *" scoped by a condition that probe doesn't satisfy (attacker CIDR, active time window, principal match, always-true Bool, unimplemented operators) evaluates False, drops out of the Z3 model, and the policy verifies as compliant. Conditions satisfiable by the attacker's own requests are invisible to the gate.

## Anchors

- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:302 verify_least_privilege (fixed probe context, no parameter to change it)
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:167 _evaluate_condition (concrete single-context evaluation), :149 operator dispatch (unknown operators → False)
- No Z3 variable ever exists for a context key (:256-258 pin action/resource only)

## Fix direction

Least privilege needs existential quantification (does ANY request context receive admin) or fail-closed UNVERIFIABLE where it can't be proven. Report proposes treating conditional Allow-*-on-* as violation-by-default (human decides if scoping is acceptable); treat as starting point. Complements (not duplicates) the H1/H5 polarity fixes — those repair verdict direction, this repairs what the probe can see.
label: SECURITY

title: [Security] IamGuard adapter admits deny-oriented risk outcomes (CWE-284)
body:
Part of tracker #62 (audit key BUG-R2-S1-A2-H5, CVSS 10.0, reproduced end to end on main).

## Summary

The to_verification_context provenance gate keeps VERIFIED only when allowed is True — correct solely for allow-oriented statements. For the README's canonical deny-oriented check ("Is it accessible from the public internet?", context 8.8.8.8), allowed=True is the risk outcome, so a publicly-accessible policy (up to full-admin wildcard, plus smuggled statements the check never queries) is the only ADMIT-able result under the documented "IAM policy is safe to apply" statement, with a valid ES256 attestation. The IP-restricted safe policy is structurally DENIED.

## Anchors

- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:390 to_verification_context gate (allowed is True direction)
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:317 to_diagnostic (both outcomes map to VERIFIED)
- README:255-262 schematic pairing the deny-oriented example with the safety statement; tests pinning the inverted composition

## Fix direction

The gate must bind ADMIT to the truth of the attested claim, not to the check-positive outcome — e.g. a polarity parameter declaring which outcome makes the statement true (default deny-oriented). Report proposes admit_on_allow=False default; treat as starting point, review adversarially (mind the H1 interaction: the two fixes must agree on what a violation looks like at every layer).
label: SECURITY

title: [Security] IamGuard least-privilege verdict inversion: full-admin policy ADMITted as compliant (CWE-863)
body:
Part of tracker #62 (audit key BUG-R2-S1-A2-H1, CVSS 10.0, reproduced end to end on main).

## Summary

verify_least_privilege() returns allowed=True for over-privileged policies (violation value), but every layer above the raw result reads it with verify_access polarity: to_diagnostic() maps it to VERIFIED/ALLOWED, mint_diagnostic_attestation() signs it, and the bridge emits ADMIT. A full-admin wildcard policy (Action * / Resource *) flows verified=True, allowed=True → VERIFIED → minted → ADMIT. Reproduced live 2026-09-14.

## Anchors

- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:302 verify_least_privilege (inverted contract, documented only in raw-result docstring)
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:20 shared constraint id (iam_guard.verify_access) — layers cannot tell the checks apart
- qwed_infra/guards/iam_guard.py:318 to_diagnostic, attestation.py:591 mint, verification_context_bridge.py:199,283 bridge
- Mirror of #58 (denials-mint-VERIFIED); defeats #58's evidence-parsing mitigation since the violation carries allowed=true

## Fix direction

Attribute results to their producing check (distinct constraint id / check tag on VerificationResult) and fail closed in to_diagnostic on violation values — a violation must never surface as VERIFIED. Report proposes a check field + per-check mapping; treat as starting point, review adversarially.

title: D12 should date the orphaned Keychain entries it counts
body:
Observed on a real Mac (macOS 26.6.2, 2026-09-14), the first time D12 met a real Keychain with real accounts. `doctor --keychain-scan` reported:

```
D12  64 Keychain credential entr(ies) belong to no known root
     service prefix: Claude Code-credentials-
     Left over from roots that no longer exist, or from roots this tool
     does not know about. The suffix is a one-way hash, so they cannot be
     traced back to a path. Harmless, but they accumulate.
```

Sixty-four is a number that makes a careful reader stop, and the finding gives them nothing to judge it with. The Keychain's own attributes do. Read with `security dump-keychain` and no `-d`, which is attributes only and never a secret, the 67 entries under that prefix broke down as:

- creation dates: 66 between 2026-04-22 and 2026-06-18, one to seven per working day, then one on 2026-09-07
- modification dates: identical to the creation dates for 64 of them, so never refreshed after the day they were made; the other three were modified on 2026-09-07 (two) and 2026-09-14 (one), and those three are exactly the tool's three live roots
- account attribute: 66 under the user's short name, one under `unknown`, which looks like a launch with no `USER` in its environment

So D12 was right: 64 dead entries from a workflow that gave Claude Code a fresh root per session for eight weeks and stopped. But it took two hand-written `security` pipelines to know that, and the whole point of the rule is that the reader should not have to.

## What to change

When D12 fires, read `cdat` and `mdat` for the matching entries from the same attribute-only dump the scan already uses, and print the range: how many entries, created between which dates, and the latest modification date, so the finding reads as evidence rather than a count. "64 entries, created 2026-04-22 to 2026-06-18, none modified since 2026-06-18" says dead; "3 modified this month" says something is alive that the tool does not know about, which is a different finding and should be worded as one. Consider a separate line for entries whose modification date is within the last 30 days.

At `--explain`, consider listing each entry's service name with its two dates, so a user who wants to clean up can do so by hand with the tool's usual `security delete-generic-password -s <service>` shape. The tool must keep never deleting them itself; this is the D12 half of the "never touches a credential" invariant, and it stays.

Test with the stand-in `security` in `tests/cases/60-credentials.sh`, which will need to emit `cdat` and `mdat` attributes in the shape the real `dump-keychain` prints them (`"cdat"<timedate>=0x... "20260618120000Z\000"`), plus a case where an orphan was modified recently and the wording changes. Record the real-machine breakdown above under F03 in `docs/FACTS.md` as the first observation of D12 against a real Keychain.

## Run with

- Model: Claude Sonnet 5 (`claude-sonnet-5`)
- Effort: `medium`

## Done when

- D12's finding states the creation range and latest modification of the orphaned entries.
- An orphan modified within the last 30 days is called out separately.
- `--explain` lists the entries with dates; nothing reads a credential value; nothing deletes.
- The stand-in `security` emits the two attributes and the tests cover both wordings.
- The 2026-09-14 breakdown is recorded in `docs/FACTS.md`.
label: SECURITY

title: Наряд №314 (P0, security/perception): egress-гейт MEDIA_EGRESS_TAINT — сценарий «кухонной камеры» end-to-end
body:
> Оценка: 2–3 д · Зависит от: №311, №312, №313 · Блокирует: №315 (диспатч волны), В2 (№316)

**Факт.** Категория-A статических гейтов — исполненный паттерн: `MODEL_WEIGHTS_UNSAFE`/`VISION_POLICY_MISSING` (`src/audit.rs:1607–1757`, №241/ADR-0125, Block 3) — statically visible violations на call-site, `Severity::Error`, Category A, блокируют сборку. Sinks сети/ответа реальны: `http_post` (`src/builtins/registry.rs:182`, с SSRF-guard №261: `is_blocked_address`, классы loopback/private/CGNAT/benchmark), `http_post_multipart` (`:183`), `respond`/`respond_html` (`:175–176`). Чего нет: медиа-хэндлы (№311) с клиренсами (№312/№313) **не связаны с sinks** — сегодня `http_post(url, image_open(...))` скомпилируется и унесёт приватный кадр наружу. Это центральный кейс плана v1.1 (§5.3, «кухонная камера») и единственный способ превратить решётку из аннотации в гарантию: **программа с утечкой не собирается**.

**Задача.**

1. Category-A гейт `MEDIA_EGRESS_TAINT` (по шаблону №1607): на call-sites `http_post`, `http_post_multipart`, `respond`, `respond_html` (список зафиксировать в ADR; расширяем) — если аргумент-выражение выводится с media-родом (`UserInput` от медиа-билтинов №311, `Consented`, `Poisoned`) И значение — хэндл MediaStore (статически определимо через binding_taint + известные конструкторы), а политика экспорта не разрешает этот род — `Severity::Error`. Политика: `METALOGOS_MEDIA_EGRESS_POLICY` (env, значения `deny-all` дефолт | `allow-consented`) + per-call escape `http_post(..., egress_policy: "allow-consented")` — явная громкая форма (прецедент escape-hatch `METALOGOS_MCP_ALLOWLIST` №268-ADR), каждое применение — audit-событие `MEDIA_EGRESS_ALLOWED` с причиной.
2. Рантайм-дубль (принцип §7.6 плана — «расхождение статического и рантайм-представления = deny + событие»): в http_post/respond на фактическом аргументе-хэндле MediaStore сверить род стора с тем, что прошёл статический гейт; расхождение (например, Poisoned получен в рантайм-каскаде №313 после обхода статического пути) → громкий отказ + `MEDIA_EGRESS_DENIED_RUNTIME` в audit-лог.
3. `media_meta(handle)` дополняется полем `egress: allowed|blocked(policy)`, чтобы программы могли ветвиться явно, а не ловить ошибки.
4. Тесты (`tests/naryad_314_egress_*.rs`): **«кухонная камера» end-to-end**: `frame = image_open("kitchen.png"); http_post("https://cloud.example/analyze", frame)` — компиляция падает с `MEDIA_EGRESS_TAINT` и текстом, называющим род и политику; тот же код с `consent_grant(...)` + политикой `allow-consented` — собирается, `MEDIA_EGRESS_ALLOWED` в аудите; после `consent_revoke` (№313) — рантайм-отказ `MEDIA_EGRESS_DENIED_RUNTIME`; Poisoned — отказ при любой политике; регресс: существующие тесты http_post/respond зелёные, SSRF-классы №261 не затронуты; crosscheck TW/VM для легального пути.

**§3.** `src/audit.rs` (Category-A гейт), `src/builtins/http.rs` (рантайм-дубль — сверить фактический файл: rg «fn builtin_http_post»), `src/server.rs`/`src/builtins/web.rs` (respond-дубль), `src/media/store.rs` (egress-поле meta), `tests/naryad_314_egress_*.rs` + фикстура `tests/fixtures/kitchen_frame.png` (генерируется в тесте программно — не бинарник в репо), `docs/adr/0153-media-egress.md` (новый ADR: список sinks, политика, escape-семантика), `docs/threat-model.md` (новая категория гейта), `REFERENCE.md` (policy-документация), `CHANGELOG.md`.

**Сделано, когда:** «кухонная камера» — красный/зелёный/красный сценарий из п.4 полностью в CI; каждое применение escape-формы оставляет событие аудита; ADR-0153 готов к утверждению; **заглушек нет: grep `todo!\|unimplemented!\|SKELETON\|not implemented` в новых/изменённых файлах — 0, CI blocking зелёный на мерж-коммите** (правило №16.0-D); в отчёте — итоговый список покрытых sinks и что осталось за границей (напр., будущие file-экспортные sinks — в ADR).

**Связь.** №311/№312/№313 (блокируют), №241/ADR-0125 (шаблон Category-A), №261 (SSRF — независимый слой, не дублируется), №268 (escape-hatch-прецедент), план §5.3/§7.6/§13.2 (M1-метрика «100% утечных сценариев ловятся компиляцией»).

title: Наряд №312 (P0, feature/perception): решётка клиренсов — Consented и Poisoned в TaintKind, композиция join
body:
> Оценка: 2–4 д · Зависит от: №311 · Блокирует: №313, №314

**Факт.** Taint-механика реальна и исполняется: `enum TaintKind { LlmOutput, Secret, UserInput, Sanitized, … }` (`src/audit.rs:119`), `TaintTracker` с `tainted: HashMap<String, TaintKind>` (`:142`) и `get_expr_taint(expr, tracker)` (`:175`) — тaint выводится по AST на call-site, Category-A проверки потребляют его (шаблон: `MODEL_WEIGHTS_UNSAFE`, `src/audit.rs:1607–1757`). Path-sensitive-прецедент уже есть: Canary-род №284 поставляется только внутри then-ветки `if (r.leaked)` (check_canary_leak). Кинов качественных родов: (а) согласия нет — `consent_ledger` voice-стора (`src/voice/store.rs:31`) отделён от taint-системы: программа не может статически выразить «данные с записанным согласием»; (б) компрометация выражается только канаречным спец-кейсом №284, а общего «отравленного» рода, которому запрещены ВСЕ sinks, не существует. Между тем стратегический план v1.1 §7.2 требует решётки `public < consented < private < poisoned` как несущей конструкции P0.

**Задача.** Ввести два рода и их честную алгебру, не ломая существующие пять:

1. `TaintKind::Consented` — данные с записанным согласием субъекта (заполняется №313; в этом наряде — род, диспатч и правила). `TaintKind::Poisoned` — компрометированные/отозванные данные: **легальных sinks нет** — каждая существующая Category-A sink-проверка (http_post, respond, reflex_train — сверить полный список по Category-A в audit.rs) расширяется правилом «Poisoned → Error» с отдельным сообщением и check_id `POISONED_SINK` (не переиспользовать чужой check_id).
2. Порядок и join: зафиксировать в коде (и ADR) частичный порядок для media-релевантных родов: `Sanitized < UserInput < Consented`, `Poisoned` — несравнимый максимум-карантин (любой join с ним даёт Poisoned). Композиция выражений (`get_expr_taint`): конкатенация/интерполяция/коллекции из значений разных родов → **join** (максимальный по порядку; наличие Poisoned в любом операнде — Poisoned). Существующие проверки не должны ослабнуть: полный прогон audit-тестов обязателен, диффа сообщений — только добавление нового check_id.
3. `binding_taint()`: `media_close` — нейтрален; `image_open/frame_open/scene_*` (№311) остаются `UserInput`; новые формы согласия (№313) лягут на `Consented` в следующем наряде — здесь достаточно рода + join + Poisoned-гейтов.
4. Диагностика: каждое новое нарушение — текст с объяснением рода и пути (конвенция существующих Category-A сообщений, включая SSRF-тексты №261).
5. Тесты (`tests/naryad_312_lattice_*.rs`): join в интерполяции (`"a" + tainted_var` — распространение); Poisoned в http_post/respond → POISONED_SINK Error; Consented в http_post → НЕ ошибка на этом наряде (согласие легально в концепт-семантике; полный egress-гейт — №314); path-sensitive: Poisoned, порождённый в ветке, не покидает ветку (по образцу check_canary_leak №284); регресс: все существующие audit-тесты без деградации.

**§3.** `src/audit.rs` (TaintKind, порядок, join, POISONED_SINK), `docs/adr/0152-taint-lattice.md` (новый ADR: порядок родов, join-семантика, отклонённые альтернативы — полностью числовой lattice / отдельная размерность), `tests/naryad_312_lattice_*.rs`, `docs/threat-model.md` (строка о решётке), `REFERENCE.md`/`CHANGELOG.md` (если появятся видимые формы).

**Сделано, когда:** тест-кейсы join и Poisoned-гейта зелёные в CI; существующие taint-тесты (№268 mcp, №284 canary, UNTRUSTED_TRAINING_DATA) без диффы поведения кроме новых сообщений; ADR-0152 готов к утверждению; **заглушек нет: grep `todo!\|unimplemented!\|SKELETON\|not implemented` в новых/изменённых файлах — 0, CI blocking зелёный на мерж-коммите** (правило №16.0-D).

**Связь.** №311 (блокирует), №284 (path-sensitive-прецедент), №261/№268 (sink-проверки), №313 (Consented-источник), №314 (egress-гейт потребляет решётку), план v1.1 §7.2/§8.3 (t ≤ maxTaint — будущий мост, не в этом наряде).

title: Наряд №313 (P0, feature/perception): ConsentLedger v2 — субъекты, scope, TTL и revoke-каскад в Poisoned
body:
> Оценка: 2–3 д · Зависит от: №311, №312 · Блокирует: №314

**Факт.** Согласие существует в одном домене: `consent_ledger` (`src/voice/store.rs:31–61` — таблица `consent_ledger (voiceprint_hash, nonce, model, timestamp)`, `record_consent` `:127`, проверка наличия записи `:142`) — плоская запись «голосовой отпечаток ↔ модель» без субъекта как сущности, без scope, без срока, без отзыва. Отзыв в языке невозможен, значит GDPR-стиль «right to erasure» не выражаем — а план v1.1 §7.4 (`ConsentGrant/ConsentRevoke`) и §10.3 (forget-каскад) требуют отзыва с каскадом. Провенанс-основа для каскада есть: `VisionManifest`/стор (`src/vision/provenance.rs`, №241, ADR-0125) связывает артефакты хэшами `model_sha256/prompt_sha256/png_sha256`; MediaStore №311 несёт `meta_json` с prov-полями. Taint-цель каскада готова: `TaintKind::Poisoned` №312.

**Задача.** Обобщить согласие до языка медиа с настоящим каскадом отзыва:

1. `src/media/consent.rs`: таблица `consent_ledger_v2 (id INTEGER PK, subject_id TEXT NOT NULL, scope TEXT NOT NULL, media_kind TEXT NOT NULL, artifact_sha256 TEXT, granted_at TEXT NOT NULL, expires_at TEXT, revoked_at TEXT)` — грант согласия привязан к субъекту + scope («голос», «изображения кухни», класс медиа) и опционально к конкретному артефакту по хэшу; TTL — реальное поле, истёкший грант = отсутствующий. Миграция: существующая voice-таблица остаётся (не ломаем №172-контур), voice-записи дублируются в v2 при первом запуске (backfill-миграция с фиксацией в отчёте).
2. Билтины: `consent_grant(subject, scope, handle?, ttl_secs?)` — записывает грант, помечает хэндл в TaintTracker родом `Consented` (№312) с сохранением связи subject→handle в сторе; `consent_revoke(subject, scope)` — линейное аудируемое действие: (а) помечает `revoked_at`, (б) **каскад**: все артефакты MediaStore/VoiceStore, производные от scope (по prov-хэшам и subject-связям) → их переменные в TaintTracker переводятся в `Poisoned` + будущие `media_meta(handle)` возвращают `revoked: true`; (в) пишет audit-событие `CONSENT_REVOKED_CASCADE` с числом затронутых артефактов.
3. Семантика «забыть нельзя обойти»: Poisoned после revoke не снимается никакой операцией в этом наряде (decontamination — будущий наряд по §7.2, здесь — честная граница «отзыв окончателен»).
4. Тесты (`tests/naryad_313_consent_*.rs`): grant → handle в TaintTracker Consented; revoke → та же переменная Poisoned → http_post на ней падает POISONED_SINK (№312-гейт); каскад по цепочке «изображение → производный scene_query-атрибут» (связь через prov-поля meta_json) помечает производный артефакт; TTL: истёкший грант не даёт Consented; персистентность: revoke переживает перезапуск процесса (SQLite); событие CONSENT_REVOKED_CASCADE присутствует в audit-логе с числом.

**§3.** `src/media/consent.rs` (новый), `src/media/store.rs` (миграция v2 + backfill), `src/voice/store.rs` (только чтение для backfill), `src/builtins/registry.rs` (2 spec!-строки), `src/builtins/mod.rs` + диспатч (конвенция №240/№311), `src/audit.rs` (Consented-постановка + cascade-хук), `tests/naryad_313_consent_*.rs`, `REFERENCE.md` (2 билтина), `docs/threat-model.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`.

**Сделано, когда:** сценарий «согласие выдано → данные Consented → согласие отозвано → тот же хэндл Poisoned → sink громко отказывает → в аудите число каскада» проходит end-to-end в CI; backfill voice-записей воспроизводим на пустой и существующей БД; **заглушек нет: grep `todo!\|unimplemented!\|SKELETON\|not implemented` в новых/изменённых файлах — 0, CI blocking зелёный на мерж-коммите** (правило №16.0-D); отчёт называет допущения (гранулярность scope, поведение при partial-хэшах).

**Связь.** №311/№312 (блокируют), №172 (voice-стор и крипта), №241/ADR-0125 (провенанс-хэши), №284 (path-sensitive), план §7.2/§7.4/§10.3 (forget в В6 опирается на этот каскад), GDPR-аргумент грантового контура.

title: refactor(mcp): replace raw Axios JSON-RPC transport with the official MCP TypeScript client
body:
## Priority

P1 / MCP transport modernization before the final native Wallet query refactors.

Suggested story points: **8**.

Implement after #143/#138/#139 and before #161/#162 so new native aggregation/search adapters are built on the steady-state MCP transport rather than on protocol plumbing that is about to be replaced.

## Summary

Replace the repository's application-owned MCP transport/protocol implementation based on Axios and hand-built JSON-RPC `tools/call` requests with the official Model Context Protocol TypeScript client and Streamable HTTP transport, while preserving the repository's Wallet-specific typed adapter, logging/redaction, financial write uncertainty, and fail-closed behavior.

The current `WalletMcpClientService` should remain the application-facing Wallet adapter. The refactor should remove protocol mechanics from that service, not remove the service itself.

## Motivation / Current Limitations

The current implementation constructs MCP JSON-RPC requests directly and manually handles transport details such as:

```text
Axios HTTP POST
  -> hand-built JSON-RPC envelope
  -> tools/call
  -> manual structuredContent/text unpacking
  -> application error classification
```

This was sufficient for the initial integration, but MCP now has a maintained official TypeScript client that owns protocol and transport concerns such as:

- Streamable HTTP transport behavior;
- MCP client lifecycle;
- protocol-version negotiation;
- tool discovery through `listTools()`;
- tool invocation through `callTool()`;
- current tool schema exposure;
- structured tool responses and evolving protocol behavior.

Maintaining those mechanics locally increases the risk that the application diverges from newer MCP protocol behavior and forces Wallet-domain work to depend on a custom protocol client unnecessarily.

The repository also currently drops useful MCP response metadata such as `_meta.rateLimit` and `agentHints` at the generic tool boundary. The transport modernization is a natural point to expose this metadata through a narrow typed adapter where it is useful without leaking arbitrary raw MCP responses across the application.

## Desired Outcome

Use the official MCP TypeScript client for protocol and transport concerns while keeping application policy and Wallet-specific behavior explicit:

```text
Application / handlers
  -> WalletMcpClientService
       -> typed Wallet adapters
       -> validation/normalization
       -> logging/redaction
       -> write outcome policy
       -> official MCP Client
            -> Streamable HTTP transport
            -> protocol negotiation
            -> listTools / callTool
```

The application should no longer construct generic MCP JSON-RPC envelopes or manually implement `tools/call` transport semantics during normal operation.

## Proposed Architecture & Design

### 1. Keep `WalletMcpClientService` as the Wallet adapter

Preserve a narrow application-facing API such as:

```text
fetchAccounts()
fetchCategories()
fetchBudgets()
fetchRecords()
createRecords()
createLabel()
verifyClientProfile()
```

and future wrappers for native aggregation/search/transfer/entity operations.

Do not expose the raw MCP client or arbitrary model-controlled tool names to higher layers.

### 2. Delegate MCP protocol mechanics to the official SDK

Replace application-owned behavior for:

- JSON-RPC envelope construction;
- generic `tools/call` request construction;
- protocol-version negotiation;
- Streamable HTTP lifecycle semantics;
- generic tool-list discovery;
- low-level structured response plumbing where the SDK already owns the contract.

Use the SDK's supported current API after verifying the exact package/version compatible with Node 22 and the Wallet MCP endpoint.

### 3. Preserve financial `UNKNOWN` semantics

The official SDK handles MCP transport, but it does not automatically own this application's financial commit-safety policy.

Keep an application-owned outcome classifier around mutation calls so uncertain network/transport failures cannot trigger blind retry:

```text
authoritative server/tool rejection
  -> DEFINITIVE_FAILURE

transport failure where server receipt/commit cannot be ruled out
  -> UNKNOWN
```

Do not reinterpret every SDK exception as safely retryable.

### 4. Add typed tool/capability discovery boundary

Expose `listTools()` through a narrow typed capability representation that #163 can consume.

Do not dynamically grant semantic/model authority based on advertised tool names.

Preferred split after this issue and #163:

```text
MCP listTools()
  -> actual available MCP tools and schemas

Wallet get_client_profile
  -> Wallet-specific scopes/permissions
  -> sync/readiness
  -> base currency/settings
```

### 5. Preserve Wallet response metadata where useful

Normalize useful generic response metadata rather than silently discarding it, especially:

- `_meta.rateLimit` when present;
- Wallet `agentHints` when present;
- other bounded metadata required by specific typed adapters.

Do not expose arbitrary upstream metadata directly to the LLM.

Rate-limit metadata may inform application pacing/diagnostics, but it must not introduce aggressive automatic retry behavior for financial mutations.

## Proposed Implementation Plan

1. Select and pin the official MCP TypeScript SDK package/version compatible with the repository's Node 22 + native ESM environment.
2. Add a small transport/client lifecycle wrapper owned by `WalletMcpClientService` or a dedicated MCP transport component if complexity warrants separation.
3. Connect to the configured Wallet MCP HTTP endpoint using the supported Streamable HTTP transport and existing bearer-token authentication.
4. Reimplement the generic internal call boundary on top of SDK `callTool()` while keeping existing typed Wallet methods stable where practical.
5. Introduce a typed `listTools()` capability-discovery method for #163 without exposing generic execution to semantic/model code.
6. Preserve application-level error classification, financial `UNKNOWN` handling, logging policy, and redaction around SDK failures.
7. Normalize `_meta.rateLimit` / `agentHints` only through bounded typed response metadata needed by consumers.
8. Add hermetic SDK-boundary fixtures/mocks and an explicit live Wallet MCP compatibility check outside default CI.
9. Remove obsolete Axios MCP transport/protocol code only after behavioral parity is verified.

## Migration / Compatibility Considerations

- Preserve the current public behavior of Wallet read/write adapters during the transport migration.
- Do not combine #161 or #162 production behavior changes into this issue.
- #161/#162 should consume the post-migration adapter rather than create a second transitional abstraction.
- Existing live MCP test entry points may be adjusted to verify SDK connectivity, but default CI remains offline/hermetic.
- Preserve bearer-token handling and ensure credentials never appear in logs or thrown error details.
- If the official SDK cannot represent a required Wallet endpoint/authentication behavior, document the concrete gap before retaining any custom protocol shim.

## Security / Safety Requirements

- Do not expose generic MCP tool execution directly to user/LLM-controlled tool names.
- Preserve the allowlisted semantic trust boundary from #117.
- Preserve deterministic entity validation before financial writes.
- Preserve `UNKNOWN` outcomes for genuinely uncertain mutation dispatches.
- Never auto-retry an uncertain financial mutation merely because the SDK reports a transport error.
- Keep access tokens redacted from logs and diagnostics.
- Respect upstream rate-limit metadata where available; do not convert it into uncontrolled retry loops.
- Runtime MCP/server authorization remains authoritative even when tool discovery advertises a capability.

## Regression Coverage

- [ ] client initialization works with the configured Wallet MCP endpoint and bearer token;
- [ ] `get_client_profile` still works through the typed Wallet adapter;
- [ ] account/category/budget/label reads preserve current normalized behavior;
- [ ] record reads preserve current application-visible behavior before #161/#162 change their internals;
- [ ] create-record success remains authoritative;
- [ ] explicit MCP/tool rejection maps to `DEFINITIVE_FAILURE`;
- [ ] ambiguous transport failure around a mutation remains `UNKNOWN`;
- [ ] no automatic mutation retry occurs after `UNKNOWN`;
- [ ] `listTools()` can be normalized without granting arbitrary semantic tool authority;
- [ ] `_meta.rateLimit` / `agentHints` can be retained when present without leaking arbitrary data;
- [ ] auth/token values remain redacted in logging/error output;
- [ ] tests remain hermetic by default;
- [ ] explicit live MCP verification remains separate from normal CI.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Normal MCP communication uses the official MCP TypeScript client and supported Streamable HTTP transport.
- [ ] Application code no longer constructs generic JSON-RPC `tools/call` envelopes for normal Wallet operations.
- [ ] `WalletMcpClientService` remains the narrow Wallet-specific application adapter.
- [ ] Existing typed Wallet read/write behavior remains compatible unless a verified MCP contract correction is required.
- [ ] Financial `DEFINITIVE_FAILURE` vs `UNKNOWN` safety semantics remain explicit and tested.
- [ ] Tool discovery is available through a bounded typed API suitable for #163.
- [ ] Generic advertised MCP tools are not automatically exposed to the semantic LLM layer.
- [ ] Useful upstream rate-limit/agent-hint metadata is not silently lost when a typed consumer requires it.
- [ ] Authentication and logging remain fail-closed/redacted.
- [ ] `npm run build`, `npm run test:vitest`, and `npm run test:offline` pass.
- [ ] Any live Wallet MCP verification is explicit and outside default CI.

## Non-goals

- Do not remove `WalletMcpClientService` or replace it with direct SDK calls throughout handlers.
- Do not implement #161 native aggregation in this issue.
- Do not implement #162 native text-search cleanup in this issue.
- Do not implement #143 native transfer semantics in this issue.
- Do not make `listTools()` a dynamic LLM tool allowlist.
- Do not move confirmation, pending state, reconciliation, or entity validation into MCP.
- Do not assume SDK transport errors make financial writes safe to retry.

## Related Work

- #117 guarded semantic trust boundary
- #121 MCP-native-first architecture umbrella
- #143 native paired-transfer / `create_records` contract alignment
- #163 typed MCP capability/permission/sync discovery
- #164 MCP capability-audit developer guardrail
- #161 native Wallet MCP aggregation
- #162 native Wallet MCP text search
- #113 incremental Vitest migration

title: Multi-device identity, and identity rotation
body:
Today a node **is** its seed: one device, one address. Two devices belonging to one person are two unrelated nodes, and there is no way to say otherwise.

Both halves are genuinely hard and related to #317:

- **Multi-device.** Either the seed is copied — which makes every device a full compromise of the identity and breaks the forward-secrecy story — or devices are separate identities linked by a statement someone has to trust
- **Rotation.** The successor-statement problem: anyone holding the old key can sign one too

## Also blocked on this

The web node's "multiple identities" screen. Every store there is keyed by app rather than by identity, so the app layer assumes one identity per node as thoroughly as the kernel does.
label: SECURITY

title: An independent security review — the empty column
body:
[`docs/SECURITY_MATRIX.md`](../blob/master/docs/SECURITY_MATRIX.md) is generated from the tree, and the **independently reviewed** column is empty for all twelve components. That is the most important cell in the table.

Every fault on record was found by the people who wrote the thing — fuzzing, property tests, a simulator, and reading. That is a real method with a known blind spot: it finds what its authors thought to look for.

## What would count

Not "someone looked at it". A review is on the table when a named person or firm has examined a named component and their findings are public, including the ones that turned out not to be findings.

## Where to point a reviewer first

By exposure, which the matrix already ranks:

1. The envelope parser — every byte of every frame, from anyone in range, before any check runs
2. `node::ingest` forwarding — whole envelopes plus the tables they grow
3. The double ratchet — two live faults were found here by property tests, which suggests the area rewards attention
4. `topic::` key schedule — group roster and rekey material from anyone already in the group

## Honest note

This is the one backlog item that cannot be closed by writing code, and the one most likely to sit here. It stays on the list because a project that says "no third-party audit" in its security policy should also say that it wants one.

title: A stolen prekey secret is a decryption oracle for its window
body:
Healing survives a stolen prekey for at most seven days, because contributions are sealed to prekeys and prekeys expire.

**Inside that window the secret opens every contribution addressed to that member.** Shortening the window is a knob, not a fix.

## What this issue is for

Deciding whether anything better is available, and writing down the answer either way.

Candidates, none obviously right:

- **Shorter window.** Cheap, and only moves the number. Also costs deliverability: a prekey that expires faster is one a delay-tolerant sender is more likely to miss, which is the whole premise of the protocol working against it.
- **Ratchet earlier.** Forward secrecy already exists for established sessions; the exposure is the one-shot seal *before* a session exists. Getting to a ratchet sooner narrows the window to the first message.
- **Accept and document.** The honest option, if the alternatives cost more than they buy.

## Constraint

Whatever is chosen must not make a node that has been offline for a week unable to receive. That is not a corner case here; it is the design.
label: SECURITY

title: Encrypted groups have no roster — the largest honest gap versus a messenger
body:
Membership of a keyed group — and therefore who a contribution is sealed to — is entirely the application's problem. The protocol has the key and nothing else.

In a partition, two halves diverge onto different keys and both keep working. `topic::key_id` makes that **legible** without resolving it: a screen can say "this group has split" rather than silently showing half a conversation.

## Why it is not simply a missing feature

Solving it properly is **distributed agreement, not cryptography**. Who is in the group is a fact two disconnected halves cannot settle without talking, and this protocol is built for the case where they cannot talk. Any roster that claims consensus is claiming something SPORE deliberately does not provide.

## What is worth doing, short of solving it

- [ ] A `key_id` divergence badge in the UI, so a split is visible rather than mysterious
- [ ] Documentation that says plainly: an encrypted group's membership is whoever holds the key, nobody can be removed, and a re-key is the only exclusion mechanism
- [ ] A decision on whether "remove a member" should exist at all as a UI concept, given that it can only mean "re-key and hope the removed member does not have the new one"

## What must not happen

A member list that looks authoritative. That is the fake-UI rule applied to a data structure.
label: SECURITY

title: Identity compromise: decide, do not drift
body:
A stolen seed signs as that address **forever**. The threat model says so plainly, and says a real answer would be a new wire feature.

That is a description, not a decision, and the difference matters to anyone choosing whether to depend on this.

## The asymmetry that makes it a decision rather than a gap

Group keys already have `rotate`, `rekey_seal` and `contribute`. Identity has nothing. Either that asymmetry is right — and the spec should say why — or it is an omission, and the successor statement should be designed.

## The two honest outcomes

**Scope it out.** Write in the spec that identity is permanent, that a compromised seed is a permanent compromise, and why: recovery implies an authority, and an authority is the thing this protocol does not have. Then say what a user should do instead (a new identity, announced out of band by a human who is trusted for other reasons).

**Or design the successor.** A signed statement binding an old address to a new one, carried like any other envelope. The hard part is not the format; it is that anyone who has the old key can sign one too, so it is only meaningful to someone who learns the new address another way — which may make it not worth the wire.

## What must not happen

Leaving it as a paragraph in the threat model that reads like a to-do. Someone building on this deserves to know which of the two answers it is.

title: No service has rate limiting — bounded today by loopback, unbounded once the web client ships
body:
From `docs/audit/AUDIT_2026-09.md` §8, finding **M-2** (2026-09-12). Medium, reasoned from code — not reproduced.

> The audit cites this finding but gives it no section of its own — see #276.

## What happens

No service and no bot has any rate limiting. A search for `RateLimit`, `AddRateLimiter` and `UseRateLimiter` across `src/` returns nothing (re-checked 2026-09-14).

## Why it is Medium and not higher, today

Every API binds to `localhost` and has exactly one trusted caller, the bot. There is currently no path by which an untrusted client can send it volume.

## Why that changes

The web client (#97) puts an internet-facing surface in front of the same APIs. From then on a missing limit is no longer bounded by topology — and it compounds H-6 (#36): the credit-ceiling race is exploited with concurrent requests, which a rate limit makes harder to land.

## Fix

ASP.NET Core's built-in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.RateLimiting` middleware on whatever becomes internet-facing — per user where the caller is identified, per IP otherwise. No third-party dependency.

## Acceptance

Before #97 ships: every internet-reachable endpoint has a limit, and a burst above it gets `429`.

## Related

#97 (the exposure), #36 (what concurrent volume exploits).


```
$ nika check secret-in-file.nika.yaml --plain
ok PLAN     1 wave · 1 task
ok SECRETS  no declared secret reaches an effect · model echo untracked
…
-> HINT     [documentation-host] task `call` fetches api.example.com — RFC 2606
ok audited · 1 task · risk supervised
layers · valid ok · run ready ok
```

The only hint is that `api.example.com` is a documentation host. The **key in the file** is invisible to SECRETS, JOURNEY, and the audit line. `ok SECRETS` is a lie in the sense a human reads it: there is a live-shaped credential in git-ready YAML.

This is the opposite of One Door honesty. The gate is precise about *declared* secrets and silent about the thing that actually leaks.

## Expected

A check finding (warn at minimum, fail under `--strict` / a `nika check` secrets-in-source policy):

- literal `sk-` / `sk-live-` / `sk-ant-` / `xai-` / `Bearer ` + long token in any scalar
- high-entropy quoted strings in `headers:` / `env:` / `exec:` argv

Message names the field, not « no declared secret ». Fix-form: move to a secret handle / env ref the journey already knows how to track. Do **not** print the token back in the finding.

JOURNEY should also stop saying `0 sources` when a header is an inline credential.

## Proof

The specimen above must not print `ok SECRETS  no declared secret reaches an effect` without a secrets-in-source finding. A declared `${{ secrets.x }}` path stays the journey; this issue is the **undeclared inline** path.

## Not this issue

- Mocking fetch under `mock/echo` ([#1605](https://github.com/supernovae-st/nika/issues/1605)).
- `api.example.com` documentation-host hint (that one is good).

title: Research proposal: threat model and requirements for signed transitions / authenticated replicas
body:
## Problem statement

The v0.6 distributed-state trust boundary is self-asserted: ADR 0015 gives every replica authority over its own history and makes divergence fail closed, but nothing authenticates who produced a transition or a replica. Signed transitions and authenticated replicas are a post-v1.0 extension candidate, and no threat model or requirements work exists for them.

## Why this matters

The project derives requirements before mechanisms — ADR 0015 rejected Raft, CRDTs, and op-shipping on requirements grounds, and the roadmap's signed-transitions item is explicitly framed as replacing the self-asserted trust boundary. Proposing authentication before modeling the adversaries and assets would repeat the mistake the distributed-state ADR avoided. This issue performs threat modeling and requirements gathering only. **Nothing is scheduled; nothing is promised** — the output feeds a future ADR.

## Technical context

- `ROADMAP.md` — post-v1.0 extensions: "Signed transitions / authenticated replicas (replaces the self-asserted v0.6 trust boundary)."
- `docs/adr/0015-distributed-state.md` — per-replica authority, fail-closed divergence, and the stated CAP posture, which define what is and is not defended today.
- `docs/spec/security.md`, `SECURITY.md` — the current posture (no network I/O by default, untrusted input, hash-verified integrity, simulation default) and the longer-term security considerations list, which names signed transitions.
- `docs/research/v1.0-review.md` — carried limitation 4: "No signed transitions/authenticated replicas."
- `docs/adr/0002-state-identity.md` and `docs/adr/0003-canonical-serialization.md` — content-addressed identity, which any signing scheme must compose with deterministically.
- `docs/research/limitations.md` — the honest-limitations framing this document must follow.

## Possible approach

Threat-model and requirements only: enumerate the assets (state store, peer sync, commit integrity), the adversaries (malicious replica, tampered store, network attacker), and the trust assumptions ADR 0015 currently makes. Analyze what fail-closed divergence does and does not defend against. Derive requirements for signature and identity primitives that remain consistent with content-addressed identity and the determinism requirement, and record the open questions and the unresolved primitives. No implementation, and no commitment that the extension will happen.

## Acceptance criteria

- A threat-model and requirements document exists under docs/research/ with an adversary/asset model, a gap analysis against the ADR 0015 posture, and derived requirements.
- The analysis states what the current design already handles versus what genuine authentication would add.
- The document states explicitly that this is threat modeling and requirements gathering, not an implementation commitment, and that nothing is scheduled.
- Open questions are recorded for a future ADR, including any primitive that remains unresolved.

**Difficulty:** Advanced.

title: Independent host-safety review of the linux-ns execution backend
body:
## Problem statement

The Linux execution path — the only code path in RAHN that touches a real network or OS — is validated by CI only. It has not been independently reviewed for host-safety, namespace isolation, or cleanup behavior. An independent adversarial review is the step that turns "our tests assert this" into "someone else checked our tests".

## Why this matters

ADR 0012 rests on a structural host-safety invariant: host-side operations are limited to `ip netns add/del rahn-*`, with all link and interface mutations running inside `ip netns exec rahn-*`. Tests assert this structurally, but structural tests can encode the same blind spot as the implementation they check. Namespace isolation, failure cleanup, and the boundary of what can reach the host are exactly the areas where a second set of eyes is worth most.

## Technical context

- `docs/research/limitations.md` — "the Linux execution path is validated by CI only".
- `docs/adr/0012-linux-ns-execution.md` — the decision: shelling out to `ip`; deterministic `rahn-<node-id>` namespace naming; the host-safety invariant; `--execute` requires `--yes-i-know`; non-Linux platforms refuse at runtime; execution stops at the first failing command; `rahn destroy` cleanup.
- `.github/workflows/ci.yml` — the `linux-execution` job (requires root for netns) and the host-safety unit tests.
- `crates/rahn-exec/` — the mapping from plans to argv, plus the host-safety tests.
- `SECURITY.md` — the private reporting path for security-sensitive findings.

## Possible approach

Perform an adversarial review of: namespace isolation (can a created topology affect anything outside its namespaces?); the host-side `rahn-*` restriction (can any non-exempt argv reach the host namespace, including through argument injection in node identifiers?); cleanup paths (interrupted runs, partial topologies, `rahn destroy`); and failure modes (first-failing-command stop, half-created state). The output is a written review report. Security-sensitive discoveries go to the maintainers privately per SECURITY.md; only non-sensitive findings become public follow-up issues. The report should not overstate: it may conclude the invariant holds, and it may conclude it does not.

## Acceptance criteria

- A written review report exists, public to the extent its findings are non-sensitive.
- Each finding is triaged as a fix, an ADR-worthy design issue, or accepted-and-documented, with a linked issue or PR.
- Security-sensitive items were routed privately per SECURITY.md and are noted as such in the public report.
- The "validated by CI only" wording in limitations.md is updated only if the review provides evidence beyond CI.

**Difficulty:** Advanced.

title: security: prevent custom headers from overriding transport routing and HTTP framing
body:
## Context

The OWASP injection/SSRF review found a gap not covered by #41. Issue #41 addresses syntactically invalid custom header names/values, but a header can be syntactically valid and still be unsafe for a generic webhook engine to let message data control.

`WebhookHttpTransport` currently tries every custom header against `request.Headers.TryAddWithoutValidation(...)` and then content headers. There is no deny-list/reserved-header policy for transport-controlled fields.

Examples of security-sensitive protocol headers include `Host` and HTTP framing/hop-by-hop headers such as `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection`, `TE`, `Trailer` and `Upgrade`.

## Security problem

A custom `Host` header can make the application-layer target differ from the URI host used for destination validation/DNS connection. In virtual-host/reverse-proxy environments this can undermine the trust assumptions of an SSRF allow/deny policy based only on `WebhookMessage.Destination`.

Allowing message data to control framing/hop-by-hop headers can also create ambiguous or handler-dependent HTTP semantics and expand request-smuggling/protocol-confusion risk.

These are different from legitimate end-to-end application headers such as `Authorization`, which consumers may need to configure deliberately.

## Impact

- possible bypass of hostname/virtual-host assumptions in destination-security policies;
- SSRF controls can validate one destination while the HTTP `Host` field selects another virtual service at the connected address;
- protocol framing can become influenced by persisted tenant/message data;
- behavior differs by HTTP version/handler/proxy, making security review difficult;
- fixing only CR/LF validation in #41 does not address dangerous-but-valid header names.

## Expected behavior

ReliableWebhooks must own routing, authority and HTTP framing headers. `WebhookMessage.Headers` should be limited to safe end-to-end application headers unless an advanced consumer deliberately replaces/customizes the transport.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A documented reserved/forbidden custom-header set is defined for the default transport.
- [ ] `Host` cannot be supplied through `WebhookMessage.Headers` under the default transport.
- [ ] Message data cannot override `Content-Length`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Upgrade` or other transport/hop-by-hop framing fields deemed unsafe for the supported HTTP versions.
- [ ] The policy is case-insensitive.
- [ ] Legitimate application headers such as `Authorization` remain supported unless there is a specific documented security reason to restrict them.
- [ ] Attempts to use reserved headers fail deterministically before network I/O and do not enter transient retry loops.
- [ ] Tests prove a custom `Host` cannot override the authority derived from `WebhookMessage.Destination`.
- [ ] Tests cover each reserved header and case variants.
- [ ] The design is coordinated with #38 so destination/SSRF policy cannot be bypassed through HTTP authority manipulation.
- [ ] The design is coordinated with #41 so syntax validation and reserved-header authorization are separate, explicit checks.
- [ ] Advanced users who truly require low-level HTTP control have a documented escape hatch through a custom transport/handler rather than weakening safe defaults.
- [ ] README/production usage documents the supported custom-header contract.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, transport tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A05:2025 – Injection**
- **A01:2025 – Broken Access Control** (when authority-based network controls are bypassed)
- **A06:2025 – Insecure Design**
label: SECURITY

title: security: bind webhook metadata to the authenticated HMAC envelope
body:
## Context

An OWASP data-integrity review of `main` found that the built-in HMAC signer authenticates only:

```text
UTF8(unixTimestampSeconds + ".") || rawRequestBodyBytes
```

The generated `X-Webhook-Id` and `X-Webhook-Event` headers are not part of the HMAC input. `Content-Type` is also outside the authenticated envelope.

The production documentation correctly warns consumers not to trust these headers for authorization/routing/idempotency unless they cross-check authoritative values embedded in the signed payload. However, this remains a known insecure-by-default footgun in the built-in signing contract.

## Security problem

A receiver that verifies the signature correctly can still be given altered unsigned metadata while the HMAC remains valid.

If a receiver routes by `X-Webhook-Event`, deduplicates by `X-Webhook-Id`, or interprets the body based on `Content-Type` without an additional application-level cross-check, an intermediary or attacker capable of modifying those headers can change receiver behavior without invalidating the signature.

The current contract therefore authenticates the body, but not the complete delivery semantics presented by the generated headers.

## Impact

- event-type substitution against receivers that route by the generated event header;
- idempotency-key substitution when receivers trust `X-Webhook-Id` directly;
- content-type manipulation while preserving a valid body signature;
- repeated custom cross-check logic is required in every receiver to recover integrity that could be provided by the signing envelope;
- the generated metadata headers can be mistaken for authenticated metadata because they are emitted alongside the HMAC signature.

## Expected behavior

The built-in signed-delivery protocol should authenticate every security-sensitive metadata field that ReliableWebhooks itself generates and expects receivers to consume, using an unambiguous, versioned canonical representation.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] A versioned canonical signing format is defined for the built-in HMAC protocol.
- [ ] The authenticated envelope includes at least timestamp, stable webhook ID, event type, content type and exact payload bytes, or a documented equivalent that provides the same integrity guarantee.
- [ ] Canonical encoding is unambiguous (for example length-prefixing or another formally specified framing), avoiding delimiter ambiguity.
- [ ] A change to webhook ID invalidates the signature.
- [ ] A change to event type invalidates the signature.
- [ ] A change to content type invalidates the signature.
- [ ] A payload or timestamp change continues to invalidate the signature.
- [ ] The receiver sample verifies the full authenticated envelope before trusting generated metadata.
- [ ] Known deterministic test vectors cover the final canonical representation.
- [ ] If backward compatibility with the current `v1=` format is retained, downgrade/version handling is explicit and cannot silently verify a weaker format when a stronger version is required.
- [ ] Documentation clearly identifies which fields are authenticated and which are not.
- [ ] Secret-provider guidance recommends scoping secrets to receiver/trust audience and avoiding secret reuse across unrelated receivers.
- [ ] Public API/protocol compatibility is deliberately reviewed before v0.1.0 so the first public release does not freeze an avoidable weaker wire contract.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, signing tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A08:2025 – Software or Data Integrity Failures**
- **A04:2025 – Cryptographic Failures**
- **A06:2025 – Insecure Design**
label: SECURITY

title: security: enforce a minimum cryptographic strength for HMAC-SHA256 signing secrets
body:
## Context

An OWASP cryptography review of `main` found that `HmacSha256WebhookRequestSigner` accepts any non-empty byte sequence as an HMAC-SHA256 secret.

The only current check is `secret.IsEmpty`. A one-byte, password-derived, or otherwise very low-entropy key is accepted and produces a syntactically valid signature indistinguishable from one created with a strong key.

The existing test vector even uses a short human-readable test secret, so the test suite does not currently encode a production-strength key expectation.

OWASP guidance for HMAC/HS256 recommends cryptographically generated secrets with strength appropriate to SHA-256 and advises keys at least as long as the output (256 bits / 32 bytes) rather than passwords or low-entropy strings.

## Security problem

The built-in signer presents HMAC-SHA256 as the secure signing implementation but does not fail closed when the configured key material is trivially weak.

This leaves a high-impact cryptographic property entirely implicit and easy to misconfigure.

## Impact

- weak shared secrets can be brute-forced offline from captured webhook requests/signatures;
- compromise of the HMAC key allows attackers to forge arbitrary signed webhook payloads;
- configuration errors are not detected at startup or first signing use;
- test/sample patterns can normalize short text secrets rather than high-entropy key material.

## Expected behavior

The built-in HMAC-SHA256 signer must enforce or explicitly validate a minimum key-strength policy suitable for production use, with 32 random bytes as the secure default expectation.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] The built-in signer rejects secrets below the documented minimum cryptographic length/strength.
- [ ] The secure default target is at least 256 bits / 32 bytes of cryptographically generated key material unless a documented standards-based rationale chooses a different threshold.
- [ ] Empty and undersized secrets fail with an actionable exception that never includes the key material.
- [ ] Exactly-minimum and longer keys are accepted.
- [ ] Sample/test secret material is replaced with deterministic 32-byte+ test vectors where relevant.
- [ ] A known HMAC-SHA256 vector remains covered after changing the test key.
- [ ] Documentation tells consumers to generate random key bytes with a CSPRNG/secret manager and not use passwords/passphrases as HMAC secrets.
- [ ] Documentation covers secret rotation and recommends different secrets for distinct trust audiences/receivers.
- [ ] Secret bytes copied by the signer continue to be zeroed after use.
- [ ] No secret value is emitted in logs, traces, metrics or exception messages.
- [ ] Public API compatibility is reviewed if the minimum-key policy is configurable.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, signing tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A04:2025 – Cryptographic Failures**
- **A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration**

Reference: OWASP guidance for HMAC SHA-256 recommends cryptographically generated secrets with adequate entropy/length and not password-derived shared secrets.
label: SECURITY

title: security: isolate delivery-scoped failures so one poison message cannot stop the dispatcher
body:
## Context

An OWASP A10-focused review of `main` found that `WebhookDispatcher.ProcessLeaseAsync` catches unexpected exceptions only to log them and then rethrows. `RunAsync` observes any failed in-flight task, captures the exception, drains remaining work and rethrows. The hosted integration returns `dispatcher.RunAsync(...)` directly from `BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync`.

This means an unexpected exception associated with one delivery can terminate the entire dispatcher/hosted worker.

## Security problem

A single malformed or adversarial delivery that reaches a deterministic exception path can become a denial-of-service trigger for all webhook processing.

Current examples include protocol-invalid message fields that are not yet validated, but the same failure mode can also occur in custom signers, secret providers, classifiers, transports or other delivery-scoped extension points.

Infrastructure-wide failures (for example a persistence backend outage during `ClaimDueAsync`) may legitimately be fatal or require host-level restart. Delivery-scoped failures should not automatically have the same blast radius.

## Impact

- one poison delivery can stop processing of unrelated healthy deliveries;
- hosted applications may stop the background service or host depending on `BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior`;
- attacker-controlled message data can become an availability attack when it reaches an unexpected exception path;
- transient extension-point failures can create a full dispatcher outage instead of being isolated/retried/dead-lettered;
- the current failure model does not distinguish delivery-scoped errors from dispatcher/infrastructure corruption.

## Expected behavior

The dispatcher must contain failures at the smallest safe scope. A failure affecting one delivery should result in a controlled state transition/retry/dead-letter decision without terminating unrelated delivery processing, while genuinely fatal infrastructure/invariant failures remain observable and can still fail fast.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] The dispatcher defines and documents which exception categories are delivery-scoped versus dispatcher/infrastructure-fatal.
- [ ] Unexpected exceptions from one delivery do not automatically terminate all in-flight and future delivery processing.
- [ ] Delivery-scoped failures are persisted using a bounded retry/dead-letter strategy or another explicit terminal policy.
- [ ] A deterministic poison delivery cannot be reclaimed/reprocessed forever without progressing toward a bounded terminal outcome.
- [ ] Persistence/claim infrastructure failures that make safe processing impossible remain visible and may still stop/restart the worker deliberately.
- [ ] Cancellation and `WebhookDeliveryStoreConcurrencyException` retain their existing ownership semantics.
- [ ] Tests enqueue one poison delivery plus healthy deliveries and prove healthy deliveries continue to completion.
- [ ] Tests cover exceptions from signer/secret-provider/transport extension points and distinguish them from store-wide failures.
- [ ] Tests cover hosted-service behavior and prove one delivery exception does not unexpectedly stop the Generic Host.
- [ ] Logs/traces expose exception type/outcome without payloads, secrets, raw destination URLs or sensitive header values.
- [ ] Retry/dead-letter metrics remain internally consistent.
- [ ] Documentation describes failure isolation and operational alerting expectations.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A10:2025 – Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions**
- **A06:2025 – Insecure Design**
label: SECURITY

title: security: validate webhook ID, event type and content type before using them in protocol headers and telemetry
body:
## Context

The OWASP review of `main` found that issue #41 covers **custom header** validation, but several other `WebhookMessage` fields also cross the HTTP/logging boundary without equivalent validation.

`WebhookMessage` currently validates only that `Id`, `EventType` and `ContentType` are non-empty/non-whitespace.

Later the transport uses:

- `ContentType` through `TryAddWithoutValidation("Content-Type", message.ContentType)`;
- `Id` as the generated `X-Webhook-Id` header;
- `EventType` as the generated `X-Webhook-Event` header.

`Id` and `EventType` are also emitted into structured logs/traces, and `EventType` is used as a metric dimension.

## Security problem

Values containing CR/LF/NUL or other invalid/control characters can pass the model boundary even though they are later used as HTTP header values and telemetry fields.

That means fixing arbitrary custom headers alone does not fully close the header/log injection surface.

`Content-Type` also has protocol grammar that is not currently parsed/validated before persistence.

## Impact

- generated-header injection/request-splitting risk from invalid `Id` or `EventType` values;
- invalid `Content-Type` values can become persisted poison deliveries;
- log/trace forging or multi-line telemetry output when control characters reach sinks;
- deterministic malformed messages can fail late in the dispatcher rather than fail fast at construction/enqueue time;
- security guarantees differ between custom headers and built-in metadata fields.

## Expected behavior

Every `WebhookMessage` field that becomes an HTTP header or telemetry value must have a clear syntactic contract and be validated before persistence.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `WebhookMessage.Id` rejects CR, LF, NUL and other disallowed control characters.
- [ ] `WebhookMessage.EventType` rejects CR, LF, NUL and other disallowed control characters.
- [ ] `WebhookMessage.ContentType` is validated as a syntactically valid HTTP media type rather than only as a non-empty string.
- [ ] Invalid values fail before a message can be persisted or dispatched.
- [ ] Generated signing headers are applied using validated values only.
- [ ] Structured logs and traces cannot receive newline/control-character injection through ID or event type.
- [ ] Tests cover CR/LF/NUL, malformed media types, valid vendor media types, Unicode/allowed event names and normal stable IDs.
- [ ] Tests prove invalid built-in metadata cannot become a poison delivery in a durable store.
- [ ] Exceptions identify the invalid field but do not echo sensitive arbitrary values unnecessarily.
- [ ] Validation rules and compatibility expectations are documented in README/production usage.
- [ ] The work is coordinated with #41 so custom headers and built-in metadata use a coherent HTTP-input validation policy.
- [ ] Public API compatibility is reviewed before v0.1.0.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A05:2025 – Injection**
- **A10:2025 – Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions**
- **A06:2025 – Insecure Design**
label: SECURITY

title: security: disable automatic cookies on the default webhook HttpClient
body:
## Context

An OWASP-focused review of `main` at `811beabeab0538aa65f68901b77fc86c5fbde095` found that the default DI integration creates a pooled `SocketsHttpHandler` with `AllowAutoRedirect = false`, but leaves automatic cookie handling enabled.

`IHttpClientFactory` pools `HttpMessageHandler` instances. Microsoft explicitly warns that pooled handlers share `CookieContainer` state and that unexpected sharing can leak cookies between otherwise unrelated uses of the client.

ReliableWebhooks is a multi-destination outbound delivery engine and does not require browser-style cookie state for its delivery protocol.

## Security problem

A webhook endpoint can return `Set-Cookie`. Because the named ReliableWebhooks handler is pooled, that cookie can be retained and automatically attached to later webhook requests that match the cookie scope.

This introduces hidden cross-request state into a component whose expected behavior is stateless delivery.

In multi-tenant deployments, endpoints under the same host/domain hierarchy or shared infrastructure can influence later requests through cookie state even though the application never explicitly configured cookies.

## Impact

- unintended cookie leakage between webhook deliveries;
- cross-tenant/request state contamination for endpoints sharing cookie scope;
- receiver-controlled state can alter future outbound requests;
- harder-to-audit delivery semantics because cookies are neither part of `WebhookMessage` nor persistence/signing contracts;
- pooled handler lifetime makes the behavior non-obvious to consumers.

## Expected behavior

The default ReliableWebhooks `HttpClient` must be stateless with respect to cookies. Automatic cookie storage/sending should be disabled by default.

Consumers that deliberately need cookie-based behavior should have to replace/customize the HTTP transport explicitly and accept responsibility for isolation.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] The default `SocketsHttpHandler` used by `AddReliableWebhooks` sets `UseCookies = false`.
- [ ] A regression test has one receiver return a unique `Set-Cookie` value and proves a later webhook request does not contain that cookie.
- [ ] Tests cover multiple requests to the same host and to related paths/domains where a shared `CookieContainer` would otherwise matter.
- [ ] No cookie state is persisted implicitly between delivery attempts by the default transport.
- [ ] Direct construction with a caller-provided `HttpClient` is documented as consumer-controlled; the library does not claim to override that client's cookie policy.
- [ ] Production documentation explicitly states that the DI default disables cookies and redirects for security/predictability.
- [ ] The change does not break custom authentication headers supplied through the supported header mechanism.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration**
- **A06:2025 – Insecure Design**

Reference: Microsoft `IHttpClientFactory` guidance warns that pooled handlers share `CookieContainer` instances and may leak cookies between unrelated parts of an application.
label: SECURITY

title: security: require HTTPS destinations by default and make plaintext HTTP an explicit opt-in
body:
## Context

An OWASP-focused review of `main` at `811beabeab0538aa65f68901b77fc86c5fbde095` found that `WebhookMessage` accepts both `http://` and `https://` destinations as equally valid production destinations.

`WebhookMessage.IsHttpDestination(...)` explicitly returns true for both schemes, and there is no transport option that rejects plaintext HTTP by default.

OWASP Top 10:2025 A04 (Cryptographic Failures) and the OWASP TLS/Web Service guidance recommend encrypting service-to-service traffic in transit. Webhook requests can contain sensitive payloads, authorization headers, stable identifiers, and replayable HMAC signatures.

## Security problem

A consumer can accidentally configure a production webhook as `http://...` and ReliableWebhooks will send it without any explicit security opt-in or warning.

On plaintext HTTP, a network attacker or intermediary can observe payloads and headers, capture a valid HMAC signature/timestamp pair for replay, and modify metadata that is not covered by the current HMAC canonical bytes.

The existence of HMAC signing does not provide confidentiality and does not replace TLS server authentication.

## Impact

- disclosure of webhook payloads and custom authorization headers;
- capture/replay of signed requests inside the receiver replay window;
- tampering with unsigned request metadata;
- no server authentication against a network MITM;
- insecure production configuration is accepted silently.

## Expected behavior

HTTPS must be the safe default for outbound webhooks. Plain HTTP should require an explicit, highly visible opt-in intended for development, loopback, or a deliberately trusted private network.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] The default transport/integration rejects non-HTTPS webhook destinations before sending any bytes.
- [ ] Plain HTTP requires an explicit configuration opt-in with a security-oriented name (for example `AllowInsecureHttp`).
- [ ] The opt-in is disabled by default.
- [ ] The runnable local sample explicitly opts in for its loopback HTTP endpoint rather than weakening the production default.
- [ ] Tests prove `https://` succeeds under defaults and `http://` is rejected under defaults.
- [ ] Tests prove the explicit opt-in allows the intended HTTP development scenario.
- [ ] The rejection is classified as deterministic/non-retryable so an insecure destination cannot create an endless retry loop.
- [ ] Documentation clearly states that HMAC does not replace TLS confidentiality or server authentication.
- [ ] Production guidance recommends TLS 1.2+ / platform-secure defaults and warns against disabling certificate validation.
- [ ] Direct `WebhookHttpTransport` construction and DI-based transport have consistent documented semantics.
- [ ] Public API compatibility is reviewed before v0.1.0 if a new option/policy is introduced.
- [ ] `dotnet format`, Release build, tests, sample E2E, CodeQL, package validation and release dry-run remain green.

## OWASP mapping

- **A04:2025 – Cryptographic Failures**
- **A02:2025 – Security Misconfiguration**

References:
- OWASP Transport Layer Security Cheat Sheet
- OWASP Web Service Security Cheat Sheet

title: security: validate custom webhook headers before persistence and transport
body:
## Context

A final quality/security review of `main` found that `WebhookMessage` accepts arbitrary custom header values and `WebhookHttpTransport` later applies them with `TryAddWithoutValidation`.

Today `WebhookMessage.CopyHeaders(...)` validates only that header names are non-empty and values are non-null. The actual transport attempts to apply the stored values later, which means invalid or malicious header content can survive enqueue/persistence and fail only when the delivery is sent.

## Problem

There are two related risks:

1. **Poison messages** — malformed header names/values can be accepted into a durable store and then fail repeatedly at transport time, potentially creating deliveries that can never succeed without manual intervention.
2. **Protocol/security risk** — `TryAddWithoutValidation` bypasses normal header-value validation. If header values contain control characters such as CR (`\r`), LF (`\n`) or NUL (`\0`), applications that accept untrusted custom headers can become exposed to HTTP request-splitting / request-smuggling style behavior depending on the underlying handler/runtime behavior.

The transport should not assume persisted custom header values are already trustworthy unless the public model enforces that invariant.

## Impact

- malformed deliveries can be persisted successfully and fail only during dispatch;
- retryable processing may repeatedly encounter the same deterministic invalid-message failure;
- consumer-controlled headers can cross a protocol boundary without explicit validation;
- security-sensitive deployments may accidentally accept CR/LF/NUL or otherwise invalid HTTP header data;
- the invariant "a persisted webhook message is syntactically sendable" is not currently guaranteed.

## Expected behavior

Custom webhook headers must be validated before they become part of a `WebhookMessage` that can be persisted or dispatched. Invalid header names or values must fail fast with an actionable exception.

The transport should use normal validated header APIs wherever possible. `TryAddWithoutValidation` should only remain where there is a documented protocol reason and after input has already been strictly validated/sanitized.

## Definition of Done

- [ ] `WebhookMessage` rejects invalid HTTP header names before the message can be persisted.
- [ ] Custom header values containing CR (`\r`), LF (`\n`), NUL (`\0`) or other disallowed control characters are rejected.
- [ ] Validation is deterministic and independent of whether delivery occurs immediately or after durable persistence/restart.
- [ ] The transport no longer relies on unvalidated arbitrary consumer input when applying custom headers.
- [ ] If `TryAddWithoutValidation` remains for any path, the input reaching it is proven to have been validated and the rationale is documented.
- [ ] Generated ReliableWebhooks headers (ID, event type, timestamp and signature) continue to override conflicting custom headers safely.
